paras: Have you ever tried to count the stars in the sky? It is not easy! Today we meet Chanda Mama, the friendly Moon, who tried to count them. We will also learn to use ‘here’ and ‘there’, find out why the Moon changes its shape, and make a wind chime.
Chanda Mama! At times round as a circle and at times different.
Chanda Mama fell asleep!
The Sun peeped out from behind the clouds. It was morning. Chanda Mama woke up in the evening. He began to count again. But he had forgotten where he had stopped!
By the time he remembered, the night was over.
However, he continued to count the stars night after night. Often, he would forget the count.
One night, he was very upset. He began to cry. “Ooohh ... Ooohh ... What is this? I am never able to complete my counting.”
On seeing his tears, the Sun smiled, “Don’t worry! Why do you cry? I can tell you how many stars there are in the sky.”
“Really? How many?” Chanda Mama was surprised.
The Sun replied joyfully, “The number of lovely children is the same as the number of stars in the sky.”
Chanda Mama was happy! Now, the Moon came out every night. He would look at the stars. He would look at the children and he would smile happily.
New words: round, count, tears

sections.heading: A. Put the sentences in the correct order. Write 1 to 6.

items.q: ( ) Chanda Mama began to cry.
( ) The Sun told him that the number of stars is the same as the number of children.
( ) Chanda Mama started counting the stars.
( ) Chanda Mama fell asleep.
( ) Chanda Mama forgot where he had stopped counting.
( ) Now the Moon came out every night and smiled at the children.

paras: Look at the picture of the night. It was a full moon night. Children had come out on the rooftop to see the Moon. Can you see an owl, a man on a path and a police car in the picture too?

items.q: 1. Does the Moon look the same every night?
items.a: No. At times the Moon looks round like a circle, and at times it looks different.

items.q: 2. What did Chanda Mama try to count?
items.a: He tried to count the stars.

items.q: 3. Why did Chanda Mama fall asleep?
items.a: He was tired and sleepy after counting so many stars.

items.q: 4. Who helped Chanda Mama?
items.a: The Sun helped Chanda Mama.

items.q: 5. Complete the sentence: The number of stars in the sky is the same as _______________________.
items.a: the number of lovely children.

items.q: 1. I call the Moon, Chanda Mama. What do you call him in your language?
items.a: Teacher note: Let children say the name in their own language (for example, Chanda Mama, Chandamama, Chand, Chandrudu). Accept all answers.

items.q: 2. Chanda Mama was not able to count the stars. What things can you not count?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, grains of sand, raindrops, leaves on a tree, hairs on the head, ants).

items.q: 3. The Moon is visible during the night. What can you see in the night sky?
items.a: Teacher note: The Moon, stars, clouds, sometimes an aeroplane or a planet. Accept other correct answers.

sections.heading: D. Can be counted easily, or too many to be counted?
sections.note: Teacher note: Your teacher reads out each item. Put each in the correct column of a two-column table (Can be counted easily / Too many to be counted). Add a table image here. Add more local examples for children to sort, and repeat each phrase two or three times instead of writing them on the board. Items: 1. Children in the classroom. 2. Flowers in a garden. 3. Books in the library. 4. Pencils in your pencil box. 5. Fingers on your right hand. 6. Children in your city or town. 7. Pages in your English notebook. 8. The hairs on your head.

items.q: Can be counted easily
items.a: Children in the classroom; pencils in your pencil box; fingers on your right hand; pages in your English notebook.

items.q: Too many to be counted
items.a: Books in the library; children in your city or town; the hairs on your head.

items.q: Flowers in a garden: which column?
items.a: Teacher note: It depends. A few flowers can be counted easily, but a big garden has too many. Let children discuss and decide.

sections.heading: E. It was a full moon night. Complete the conversation using the help box.
sections.note: Help box: a camera for the picture, so bright and big, says the full moon looks very beautiful, let’s take a picture.

items.q:
Govind: Wow, look!
Safura: The moon looks so big and bright.
Sukanya: Isn’t it?
Dhruv: My grandfather ______________________.
items.a: says the full moon looks very beautiful

items.q:
Ramani: Let us take a picture.
Safura: My mother has ______________________.
items.a: a camera for the picture

items.q: Dhruv: Come. Stand here and ______________________.
items.a: let’s take a picture
so bright and big

paras: Here and There!
Look at the following sentences.
We are here on the Earth. The Moon is there in the sky.
I have a sharpener here in my pencil box.
The crayons are there in the big box.
The words ‘here’ and ‘there’ tell us about the location of things. The distance of the objects from the speaker helps us in choosing between ‘here’ and ‘there’.
We use ‘here’ to tell the location of things that are near us. Similarly, ‘there’ is used to tell the location of things that are far from us.

sections.heading: F. Fill in the blanks with ‘here’ or ‘there’. One has been done for you.

items.q: The students are playing kabaddi ________.
items.a: there (done for you)

items.q: ________ is your shirt.
items.a: Here (the shirt is near the speaker)

items.q: ________ is my bicycle.
items.a: There (the bicycle is far from the speaker)

items.q: I went to Chandigarh last year. My brother lives ________.
items.a: there

items.q: This is my bench. I sit ________ with my friends.
items.a: here

sections.heading: G. More practice. Fill in the blanks with ‘here’ or ‘there’.

items.q: 1. The stars are ________ in the sky.
items.a: there

items.q: 2. My bag is ________ on my desk.
items.a: here

items.q: 3. The school bus is ________ at the gate, far from us.
items.a: there

items.q: 4. Come and sit ________ next to me.
items.a: here

items.q: 5. Look! The Moon is ________ above the tree.
items.a: there

items.q: Point to something near you and say a sentence with ‘here’. Point to something far from you and say a sentence with ‘there’.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept any correct sentence. Sample: My pencil is here. The door is there.

paras: Chanda Mama looks round like a circle at times, and different at other times. Why? Let us find out. You will need a torch, a ball and a dark room. Never look directly at the Sun, because it can hurt your eyes.

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Why does the Moon change its shape?
sections.note: Teacher note: Darken the room. One child stands in the middle and is the Earth. A torch on a table is the Sun. The child holds a ball at arm’s length, which is the Moon. The child turns slowly in a circle, keeping the ball in front. The child watches how much of the ball is lit by the torch. The ball is always half lit. We see a different part of the lit half as the Moon moves around us.

items.q: What does the torch stand for? What does the ball stand for? Who is the Earth?
items.a: The torch is the Sun, the ball is the Moon, and the child is the Earth.

items.q: Does the lit part of the ball look the same from every place? Describe what you see.
items.a: No. Sometimes we see a thin curve, sometimes half, and sometimes the whole ball lit. Children should describe what they actually see.

items.q: Does the Moon make its own light?
items.a: No. The Moon shines because sunlight falls on it and bounces back to us.

items.q: Match the shape with its name: a thin curve, a half circle, a full circle.
items.a: A thin curve is a crescent moon, a half circle is a half moon, and a full circle is a full moon.

items.q: About how many days does the Moon take to change from one full moon to the next full moon?
items.a: About 30 days, which is about one month.

sections.heading: Physics Corner: The Moon is far away

items.q: The Moon is about 3,84,400 km away from the Earth. Is it near or far? Use the word ‘there’ in a sentence about the Moon.
items.a: It is far away. Sample: The Moon is there in the sky, very far from us.

items.q: On the Moon, things weigh much less than on the Earth, because the Moon pulls things down with less force (it has weaker gravity). A child who weighs 30 kg on the Earth would weigh about 5 kg on the Moon. What would the child be able to do on the Moon that is hard on the Earth?
items.a: Jump much higher and farther. (Teacher note: Weight on the Moon is one-sixth of the weight on the Earth.)

items.q: Stars look tiny, but each one is a huge ball of burning gas like the Sun. Why do they look so small?
items.a: Because they are very, very far away from us.

items.q: We cannot see the stars in the daytime, even though they are still there. Why?
items.a: The Sun is so bright that its light hides the faint light of the stars.

items.q: Why do stars seem to twinkle at night?
items.a: Because their light passes through moving air before it reaches our eyes. (Teacher note: Stars twinkle, but planets usually shine with a steady light.)

items.q: The picture of the night shows an owl. Name two animals that are active at night.
items.a: Owls and bats. (Teacher note: Also accept cats, foxes, hedgehogs and moths.)

items.q: Why can an owl see well in the dark?
items.a: It has very big eyes that take in a lot of light.

items.q: Why do people sleep at night? How many hours should a child of your age sleep?
items.a: Sleep rests our body, helps us grow and helps us think well the next day. A child needs about 9 to 11 hours of sleep. Children should answer in their own words.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Big numbers and counting stars

items.q: Write these numbers Chanda Mama counted in words: 311, 516, 890.
items.a: Three hundred eleven; five hundred sixteen; eight hundred ninety.

items.q: What is the number that comes right after 999?
items.a: 1000 (one thousand).

items.q: Write 516 as hundreds, tens and ones.
items.a: 5 hundreds, 1 ten and 6 ones.

items.q: Arrange from the smallest to the biggest: 516, 99, 890, 311, 100.
If Chanda Mama counts 100 stars every night, in how many nights will he count 1000 stars?
items.a: 1000 divided by 100 = 10 nights.

items.q: Count in tens up to 100: 10, 20, 30, ...
Moon diary: For one week, draw the shape of the Moon you see at night. Tally how many nights you could see the Moon and how many nights you could not.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary with the sky and the date. If the sky is cloudy, children may not see the Moon on some nights. Help children count the tally marks.

paras: Project Work: Wind Chimes. Let us make ‘Wind Chimes’ with the shapes of the moon and the stars. Follow the instructions stepwise.
Materials required: 1. Two cardboard sheets. 2. Coloured paper. 3. A pair of scissors (child-friendly scissors to be used under adult supervision). 4. A marker. 5. Thread. 6. Glue.
Step 1: Take a cardboard sheet. Cut a crescent-shaped moon from it as shown in the picture.
Step 2: Draw stars on cardboard and cut them.
Step 3: Use paper to decorate the sun.
Step 4: Attach all the above shapes as shown in the picture using thread and glue.
Our beautiful ‘Wind Chimes’ are ready.

sections.heading: I. Talk about your wind chime.

items.q: Put the steps in the correct order: (a) Attach the shapes with thread and glue. (b) Decorate the sun. (c) Cut a crescent-shaped moon. (d) Draw stars and cut them.
items.a: (c), (d), (b), (a), that is, cut the moon, draw and cut the stars, decorate the sun, and attach everything.

items.q: Write 3 to 4 sentences about how you made your wind chime. Use the words first, next, then and finally.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept any correct sequence. Sample: First, I cut a crescent moon from cardboard. Next, I drew and cut stars. Then I decorated the sun. Finally, I tied everything with thread.

sections.heading: Science Corner: Wind and sound
sections.note: Teacher note: Hang your wind chime near an open window or use a fan. Hang a few metal spoons or old keys on a stick with thread, so children can compare the sound with the paper chime.

items.q: What makes your wind chime move?
items.a: The wind, which is moving air, pushes it.

items.q: A wind chime made of metal makes a ringing sound, but your paper and cardboard chime does not. Why?
items.a: Hard metal pieces hit each other and shake (vibrate), and that makes a sound. Soft paper and cardboard do not vibrate enough to make a ringing sound.

items.q: Name two things that can make a ringing sound when struck.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, a metal spoon, a bell, a steel plate, a glass bottle).

items.q: You hang 3 threads and tie 4 stars on each thread. How many stars are there in all?
items.a: 3 x 4 = 12 stars.

items.q: Fold your decorated sun in half. Do the two halves match? What do we call this?
items.a: Yes, they match. This is symmetry. Teacher note: A circle has many lines of symmetry.

items.q: Name the shapes used in your wind chime. Which of them is round like a circle?
items.a: A crescent (moon), a circle (sun) and stars. The sun is round like a circle.
